summary:
Mission Architect is a first-person learning game that takes players through the work of planning and operating a science mission. In a five-wall flight operations room, players choose a mission, build a spacecraft, and resolve engineering checks for mass, power, propulsion, communications, and cost. After launch, they command an orbital transfer, deploy a science payload, collect data, and manage the communications link to return it to Earth. The final evaluation shows mission progress, resources, and command history.

The game is designed to make spacecraft trade-offs easier to understand through play. Its Earth-orbit missions use a simplified two-body simulation; the Moon mission uses a delta-v budget approximation. Component specifications and mission budgets are fictional, and the game does not use a live NASA data feed.
details:
NASA Mission Architect is a browser-based, first-person game about planning a space mission. Players explore a five-wall mission room with a flight-control display and four numbered workstations, each reached by turning 72 degrees. They choose a science objective, configure a spacecraft, balance engineering needs such as mass, propulsion, power, and communications, then launch and manage a simulated mission. The final mission screen visualizes the spacecraft’s orbit, health, telemetry, and events.

The game makes mission planning approachable and shows how engineering choices affect readiness and operations. I hope it sparks students’ interest in space science while encouraging problem-solving and systems thinking.

I developed the concept for Team OptimusEra and guided AI as a coding assistant while building the game, since I’m an eighth grader with limited coding experience. I used HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, and published it with Cloudflare Pages. I focused on clear controls, recognizable workstations, useful mission feedback, and graphics that run in a web browser.
